sense: dedication to a task, a cause or a person

terms.gloss: zeal, eager and steady application, commitment
terms.grammar: noun, second declension; studium alicujus reī, commitment to something
evidence: Cic. Inv. 1.36: studium est animī assidua et vehemēns ad aliquam rem applicāta magnā cum voluntāte occupātiō (Lewis & Short)
Cic. Sen. 22: modo permaneat studium et industria
terms.comment: Cicero’s definition is the English word: the mind’s steady, vigorous application to something, with a will. It is also goodwill towards a person, and very often a pursuit or a study (studia, one’s studies). For a promise one has made, see promise.

terms.grammar: participle of dēdō as an adjective, with the dative
terms.comment: Lewis & Short: “given up to, addicted, devoted to something; eager, assiduous”, especially frequent in Cicero, and used of bad things as of good. The verb dēdō is to give up, surrender.

phrases.latin: manent ingenia senibus, modo permaneat studium et industria
phrases.english: the old keep their wits, provided their commitment and hard work last

phrases.latin: vīdī fīlium tuum dēditum optimīs studiīs summāque modestiae fāmā
phrases.english: I saw your son committed to the best studies and with the highest reputation for good conduct

phrases.latin: nē exspectēmus quidem, dum rogēmur; studium semper adsit, cūnctātiō absit
phrases.english: let us not even wait to be asked; let there always be eagerness and never hesitation
